title: Cursor-Based Text Editor
statement:
Build the core of a plain text box with a cursor. The cursor always sits between two characters, or at either end, and it can never leave the text.

  • TextEditor() starts with empty text and the cursor at position 0.
  • addText(text) inserts text at the cursor. The cursor ends up right after the inserted text.
  • deleteText(k) deletes up to k characters to the left of the cursor, like pressing Backspace k times. It returns how many characters were actually deleted.
  • cursorLeft(k) moves the cursor left by up to k positions, stopping at the start. cursorRight(k) moves it right by up to k, stopping at the end. Both return the last min(10, L) characters to the left of the cursor after moving, where L is how many characters are to its left.

Every call must cost time proportional to its k or its text length, not to the length of the whole document.

Tests are a list of operations and their arguments; the first creates the editor. The expected output has one entry per operation (null where nothing is returned).

examples.why: "planet" minus 3 is "pla", plus "ce" is "place". Two steps left the cursor sits after "pla". Deleting 5 only removes the 3 characters that exist, leaving "ce" with the cursor at the start.
After moving, at most the last 10 characters left of the cursor are returned. Moving right by 5 stops after 1 step at the end of the text.

constraints: text has only lowercase English letters
hints: Storing the text as one string makes every insert and delete copy the whole document. What changes near the cursor only?
Split the text at the cursor into two parts. All edits happen at the end of the left part and the start of the right part.

Keep the left part as a stack (its top is the char just left of the cursor) and the right part as a stack in reverse (its top is the char just right of it). Moving the cursor pops from one and pushes onto the other.

explain.intuition:
Everything an editor does happens at the cursor. So split the text there into two stacks: left holds the characters before the cursor, with the nearest one on top, and right holds the characters after it, also with the nearest one on top (so it is stored reversed).

Typing pushes onto left. Backspace pops from left. Moving the cursor one step left pops a character from left and pushes it onto right, and moving right does the opposite. Each action touches only k characters, however long the document is. This is the same gap-buffer idea that real editors and contenteditable implementations use under the hood.
steps: Keep two arrays used as stacks: left and right.
deleteText(k): pop min(k, left.length) characters from left and return that count.
cursorLeft(k): move min(k, left.length) characters from left to right. cursorRight(k): move min(k, right.length) characters from right to left.
After a move, return the last min(10, left.length) characters of left, joined in order.
pitfalls: Storing right in normal order. Popping then takes the far end of the text instead of the character next to the cursor.
Returning the first 10 characters of the text, or the 10 characters after the cursor. It is the 10 just before the cursor.
Returning k from deleteText instead of the number of characters really deleted.

complexity.time: O(k) or O(text length) per call

solutions.title: One string and a cursor index
solutions.idea: Keep the full text and a cursor index. Each edit rebuilds the string with slices, which copies the document every time.

solutions.title: Two stacks around the cursor
solutions.idea: left holds the text before the cursor, right holds the text after it in reverse. Every operation only pushes and pops near the cursor.
solutions.time: O(k) or O(text length) per call

followups: Add undo for the last edit. What extra information does each stack operation need to record?
Support selecting a range and deleting it in one call. Does the two-stack design still hold up?
